content: Researchers need a standalone application for playing and extending combinatorial games based on triangulations. Players with varying technical experience should be able to choose among several game types and play alone, against computer-controlled opponents, or with another person through an accessible graphical interface. Game developers should also be able to define new games and make them available without modifying the original application.

The main need is to give researchers and students a way to explore these games interactively, so they can test ideas, observe outcomes, and extend the rules without rebuilding everything from scratch. In our context, the triangulations are a way to model and study combinatorial game behavior in a more hands-on, visual way. We also want it to be usable for teaching, so people who are not deep into the theory can still play and understand the mechanics.

Success would mean people can quickly set up a game, understand what is happening on the board, and try different strategies without friction. For research, it would let us prototype new game variants and compare behavior across them; for teaching, it would make the concepts visible enough that students can learn by playing; and for engagement, it would keep users interested because they can play alone, challenge another person, or face a computer opponent. If new games can be added cleanly without changing the core app, that would be a big sign it’s working well.

It should respond immediately from the player’s point of view, basically as soon as the move is entered. If the move is valid, the board should update right away so the result is obvious, and if it is invalid, it should clearly reject it with a visible message or highlight showing why. We’d want that feedback to feel instantaneous, not something that leaves the player waiting or guessing.

For normal play, I’d expect the application to wait for the full rule check before showing the outcome, because we don’t want it to display something misleading. That said, if an AI move or a very complex rule evaluation takes a bit longer, it’s fine to show a brief “thinking” or processing state so the user knows it’s working. I wouldn’t want the app to approximate the result unless that was clearly labeled as a preview, which I don’t think is our default need.

It should work fully offline after installation, because a lot of the expected use is in labs, classrooms, or research settings where internet access may not be reliable or even allowed. In practice, users should be able to launch it locally, play games, and load any games that are already installed on that machine without depending on a server. If there are shared game definitions, those would need to be distributed ahead of time rather than fetched during normal use.

The main expectation is a normal desktop application installed on a user’s machine, since that fits classrooms and research labs best. A portable setup from removable media could be useful too, but I’d treat that as a nice-to-have rather than a core requirement. The key point is that it should run locally and self-contained, without needing a separate backend service.

I don’t have a strict preference for a specific framework yet. What matters most is that it supports a good graphical interface, runs reliably on common desktop systems, and makes it practical to add new game definitions later. If your team has a recommendation that meets those goals, I’d be open to it.

Yes, we should definitely account for licensing. I’d prefer that any framework or bundled components have permissive terms that won’t make it hard to distribute the app to researchers and students, and we should avoid anything that would force us to open-source the whole project unless that’s explicitly intended. If third-party libraries are included, we’d need to be sure their licenses are compatible with academic and institutional use.

It would mainly handle local game state, saved sessions, user preferences, and possibly custom game definitions or logs if those are enabled. Since this is a research and classroom tool, I’d want that data kept on the machine by default and not shared anywhere unless the user explicitly chooses to export it. Basic protection like file permissions and not writing sensitive data unnecessarily should be enough in the normal course of use.

I’d keep it completely open for anyone using the machine. We don’t really need sign-in or role-based access for the core use case, since the application is meant to be easy to launch and use in shared environments. If there were future admin-style features for managing installed games, that might be separate, but it shouldn’t get in the way of normal play.

I’d see the game developer as responsible for creating the new game definition and making sure it follows the expected rules and interface so it can be loaded by the app. The researcher or end user should mostly just be able to select, play, and evaluate the game without needing to know how it was built. If there’s a validation step before a new game becomes available to others, that would usually sit with whoever is maintaining the game library rather than the normal player.

They should be able to view the rules and basic setup information before starting, and maybe adjust allowed play settings like opponent type or match options if the game supports that. I wouldn’t want normal players editing the underlying game definition during play, since that could make results inconsistent. Inspecting the definition itself could be okay in a read-only way for advanced users, but it should stay separate from anything that changes the game.

Yes, that would be important. Beginners should get a clearer guided experience, with simple explanations, highlights of legal moves, and maybe confirmations before they commit to a move, while advanced users should be able to move faster and see more detail if they want it. Accessibility-wise, I’d want the interface to be usable with keyboard navigation and readable enough for people who aren’t technical, since the audience will be mixed.

It should support full keyboard navigation, including moving focus around the board, selecting and deselecting elements, and confirming or canceling moves without needing a mouse. Help, rules, settings, and game selection should also be reachable from the keyboard in a predictable way. I’d also want shortcuts for common actions if they don’t get in the way of clarity for new users.

At launch, I’d expect a small set of representative triangulation-based games rather than a huge library. At minimum, it should include one or two standard games that researchers already care about, plus enough variation to show that the system can handle different rules and play styles. The exact list would depend on what the research team wants to compare first, so I’d need to confirm the priority games with them.

Yes, at least a few configurable rule variations would be useful at launch, especially if they’re common within a game family. Things like alternate move restrictions, optional starting conditions, or whether certain special moves are allowed would make the tool much more flexible for researchers. I wouldn’t want it overloaded with every possible variant immediately, but it should be built so those kinds of options can be added cleanly.

It should at least have a clear name, a short description, the author or source, and a version number so people can tell different revisions apart. I’d also want some way to tag or group it by game family or type, and ideally indicate compatibility with the app version if that matters. That would make it much easier for researchers to browse and for developers to maintain multiple game definitions over time.

Yes, I’d want crash logs and diagnostic data treated more carefully than normal saved games, because those can accidentally contain details people didn’t intend to share. Separating those logs from regular game data and giving them a shorter retention period would make sense, and exports should probably be written only when the user explicitly chooses to create them. I don’t know that we need encryption for everything locally, but if any files include personal or sensitive research data, then that would need to be reviewed.

I’d prefer it stay read-only for the duration of a match. If the definition changes underneath an active game, it could make results hard to trust or even invalidate a session, which would be a problem for researchers. Any edits to the game definition should apply only to new sessions, not the one already in progress.

Yes, that would be helpful. Supporting alternate names and localized descriptions would make browsing easier for different audiences, and search should be able to find a game by any of its accepted names. When a user is browsing, the app should show the name in their preferred language if available, but still keep a stable primary identifier underneath so packages don’t get confused.

I’d lean toward one canonical rule description inside the package, with translations handled for display where possible. That keeps the actual rules unambiguous and easier to maintain, especially if the package is reused across different sites or teams. If alternate phrasings are needed, they should probably be clearly marked as explanatory text rather than a second source of truth.

Solo play should just follow the game’s normal turn order, with the system advancing turns automatically as needed. For human versus human, I’d expect straightforward alternation between the two players, unless a specific game family defines a different starting rule. For human versus computer, the computer should behave like a normal player in the turn sequence, and any special exception like going first or choosing sides should be explicit in the game setup rather than assumed.

The main thing is that it needs to clearly represent the exact state of the triangulation so researchers can see what moves are legal and what the current position means. It should support typical play situations like starting from an initial triangulation, making a move, undoing a move if that’s allowed, and detecting when the game is finished. I’d also want it to handle any state changes that come from a special rule or variant without losing the ability to reconstruct the position later.

I’d expect a common abstract model rather than one fixed visual layout. The core should probably represent vertices, edges, and faces in a way that lets different triangulation-based games define their own move rules on top of it, since the games may not all use the same geometry or board shape. If there’s already a standard triangulation representation your team prefers, I’d be open to that, but I don’t know that we’ve locked one in yet.

We’d want to capture the exact move history, not just the final board shape, so the system can reconstruct how it got there. That includes the applied move, any variant-specific effects, and the game state flags that matter for legality or turn progression. If a rule changes the meaning of the position, it should also record enough metadata to explain that rule context later, otherwise the state won’t be auditable.

At minimum, I’d want a computer opponent that can play a legal move without crashing and finish a game against a person. It should be competent enough to follow the rules consistently, even if it’s not especially strong. Anything beyond that, like adjustable difficulty or deeper strategy, would be a nice enhancement but not the baseline requirement.

Yes, it should at least stop cleanly at the end of a game and recognize when no legal move exists. If a game allows passing, then it should pass rather than force an illegal move; if passing is not part of the rules, then it needs to report that it has no move and end appropriately. I wouldn’t require resigning for the minimum version unless one of the game types specifically uses that rule.

It should end the game and clearly tell the player that the computer has no legal moves. If the rules define that as a loss, win, or draw, the product should apply that outcome automatically rather than leaving it ambiguous. I’d also want a plain message in the interface so the player understands why the game stopped.

We’d need the package to make its licensing clear up front, especially if it includes third-party code or assets. For academic or institutional use, I’d want to avoid anything with restrictive terms that prevent us from running, sharing, or archiving the game definition internally, so incompatible licenses should be rejected. If the package is just a game definition layered on top of our framework, that’s easier, but I’d still want the submitter to declare any bundled dependencies and their terms.

I’d lean toward keeping the update under user control rather than silently replacing it. If a new version could change rules or saved states, automatically overwriting the old one might break ongoing games or reproducibility, so I’d prefer the product to preserve the existing version unless the user explicitly chooses to update. If side-by-side versions are feasible, that would be even better for researchers who need to compare versions.

At minimum, it should skip clearly illegal actions and retry with another legal move if one exists. It should only stop and report an error if it can’t determine any legal move or if the game state itself looks invalid. For normal edge cases, I’d rather it keep playing than interrupt the user.

If we’re actively troubleshooting a defect, we should keep the relevant logs longer until the issue is resolved. I’d also keep them longer if there’s a specific audit or compliance reason, but otherwise I’d prefer the normal shortened retention period for privacy and simplicity. For research use, I’d only extend retention if the data is clearly anonymized or the user has agreed to it.

They should be able to add and remove games, and also enable or disable them so the normal player only sees the approved set. Those controls should be available in a separate management area, not during an active game, so regular play isn’t disrupted. I’d expect them to be limited to someone with permission to manage the installation, though I’m not sure yet whether that means a full admin role or just a local curator role.

At minimum it should have a game name, a version, and enough information for the system to identify who made it and what it depends on. I’d also want supported player counts and a short rules summary so admins can tell what they’re approving without opening the package. Compatibility checks should be included too, but I’d treat those as validation results rather than just metadata.

Let’s record it as tentative for now. I know there should be some permission boundary, but I’d like to verify whether we need a distinct curator role or if existing admin permissions are enough before we lock that down.

It should capture exact player counts wherever possible, because that’s the clearest for both admins and the UI. If a game genuinely supports a range, then the range should be explicit, but I’d want to avoid vague values unless the game really needs them. For different modes or variants, it should allow separate player-count entries per mode so the package can describe them accurately.

It should label each entry with the mode or variant name and keep the player count attached to that label. That way, the UI can show something like standard mode versus advanced mode without mixing the counts together. If there are multiple variants, the package should be structured so each one is clearly separate and named consistently.

Yes, undo should be supported only if the game definition explicitly allows it, because some variants may not want reversibility. Variant-specific state changes need to be part of the recorded game state, not just the move history, so we can rebuild the position correctly later. And the game end condition should be stored clearly with the final state, so we can tell whether the game ended normally, by resignation, or by some variant-specific rule.

It should record the end reason as a distinct field, along with any winner or draw result if that applies. If more than one condition could technically be true, the system should store one primary reason and any secondary flags only if they matter to the rules, so there’s no ambiguity when reviewing the record later. I’d also want a timestamp and the final move that triggered the end, if available, because that helps reconstruct what happened.

Yes, there should be some differences by mode. In human-versus-computer play, the system should clearly identify whether the human or the computer won, and if the game can end in a draw that should be recorded too; in solo play, I’d expect the result to be tied to the player’s completion of the objective rather than a win-loss structure unless the game rules say otherwise. The trigger should always be the actual action or rule event that ended the game, whether that was a move, a resignation, or the computer reaching a terminal state.

I’d like the launch set to include a small mix that shows the range of the system rather than just the most popular one or two. The practical criteria should be things like whether the game is well understood by researchers, whether it exercises different triangulation rules or player counts, and whether it is stable enough that users can actually play it without constant clarification. I don’t have the exact final list yet, so I’d want to confirm it with the research team before locking it in.

A game should only be eligible if its rules are sufficiently settled, the triangulation behavior is unambiguous, and it can be played end to end without depending on missing external assumptions. If a game still has active rule disputes, incomplete definitions, or requires custom one-off support that would weaken the general platform, I’d rule it out for launch. I’d also exclude anything that isn’t stable enough to be packaged and reused by other developers without extra intervention.

I’d prefer a defined set of reviewers rather than “any contributor,” because game definitions need some consistency before they go into the package. In practice that would usually mean the game designer or researcher responsible for the rules, plus whoever is maintaining the platform integration, and possibly a domain reviewer if the variant is more specialized. If someone else has the right context, they can provide input, but I wouldn’t want sign-off to be completely open-ended.

I’d want the game definition to require approval from the responsible rules owner and the platform/integration reviewer at minimum, with both needing to sign off for release. A specialized domain reviewer should be mandatory only when the game falls outside the core set or uses unfamiliar rules, and their approval would be required before the definition can be published. If there’s disagreement, it should be blocked until the reviewers resolve it rather than letting one person override the others.

The cleanest path would be to return it to the author with the specific issues documented, then let the reviewers re-check it after revisions. If the disagreement is about a rule interpretation rather than a simple correction, I’d expect a short adjudication step with the research lead or designated owner making the final call. Publication should stay blocked until that decision is recorded, so we always know why the definition was accepted.

It should be ready only if the package imports cleanly, the game definition validates against the expected format, and the core gameplay can be instantiated without missing assets or unresolved rule references. I’d also want at least one successful test run through the main play paths, including whatever end-state conditions the game supports, before it’s released. If any of those checks fail, it should be held back until the issues are fixed.

The system should block illegal moves immediately, and it should explain in plain language why the move is invalid so the player isn’t left guessing. If there is a clear legal alternative, like a different edge or triangle choice, I’d like it to suggest that, but only as a helper rather than automatically correcting the move. For minor rule violations and hard-invalid moves, the behavior can differ in wording, but both should stop the action before it changes the game state.
